name: SBI Clerk
fullName: State Bank of India – Junior Associates (Customer Support & Sales) Recruitment
conductingBody: State Bank of India (Central Recruitment & Promotion Department)
eligibility: Graduate in any discipline; 20–28 years as on 1 Apr 2026 (relaxation for reserved categories); knowledge of the local language of the state applied for

notification.summary: SBI Junior Associate 2026 (Advt. CRPD/CR/2026-27/17, ≈7,680 regular vacancies, plus a separate SC/ST/OBC backlog drive CRPD/CR/SPLDRIVE/2026-27/16) closed registration on 31 Aug 2026. Regular prelims were held on 26–27 Sep 2026; the prelims result is awaited and mains is tentatively in late Nov 2026. Figures are from news/job portals (vacancy counts vary between sources); the SBI careers page could not be opened from the research environment.

importantDates.event: Local Language Proficiency Test / final result

pattern.notes: 20 minutes per section with separate timers. No sectional cut-off; state- and category-wise overall cut-off. Prelims is qualifying only; final selection is on mains marks (190 Qs/200 marks) followed by a local language test.

trendAnalysis.summary: SBI Clerk prelims is easy-to-moderate with good attempts usually in the 70s. Numerical Ability is mostly speed-based: 10–15 simplification/approximation questions, a missing/wrong-number series, one DI set and short arithmetic problems. Reasoning has 3–4 small puzzles (linear row with vacant seats, floor-colour, box, day-based) worth 12–15 questions plus syllogism, inequality, coding, blood relations, direction and alphanumeric series. English centres on one RC (7–10 Qs), cloze, error spotting, fillers and sentence rearrangement; spelling and connector questions appear occasionally.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from shift-wise memory-based analyses of SBI Clerk (Junior Associate) prelims of the 2023 cycle (Jan 2024), the 2024 cycle (Feb–Mar 2025) and the 2025 cycle (Sep 2025) published by coaching sites (Time4Education, Physics Wallah, Adda247), cross-checked with the official SBI prelims pattern. Patterns are paraphrased in our own words; no real question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: RC set (about 300–400 words, simple social/economic theme): identify the central idea or the most suitable title; distractors are partial details
RC fact-check: 'Which of the following is true / NOT true according to the passage' — one option distorts a qualifier (some→most, may→will) or reverses cause and effect
RC inference with statements I, II, III and combination options (Only I / Only I and III …); the trap statement overstates what the passage says
RC vocabulary-in-context: synonym or antonym of a word used in the passage, with distractors that are dictionary meanings not fitting the context
Passage cloze with numbered blanks; five same-part-of-speech options where distractors are look-alike or collocation-breaking words
Sentence split into parts (A)–(D) plus 'No error' (E); errors in subject–verb agreement, prepositions, pronouns, tense, comparatives, or inversion after negative adverbs
Double filler: two blanks in one sentence, five word-pairs where one word of each wrong pair fits but the other does not
Single filler: one blank, five words close in meaning; only one matches the tone/collocation of the sentence
Para jumble of five or six sentences on one theme; choose the correct order (options are sequences); connectors like 'however', 'as a result' and pronouns fix the order
Para jumble asking which sentence comes FIRST / THIRD / LAST after rearrangement (options are sentence letters)
Word swap: four highlighted words in a sentence; identify the pair whose interchange makes the sentence correct, or 'No interchange required'
Phrase replacement: a highlighted phrase with a grammar/idiom error; choose the correct replacement, or 'No replacement required'
Vocabulary & spelling: choose the correctly or incorrectly spelt word among five commonly confused spellings, or a simple synonym/antonym
Connector: choose the word/phrase that joins two sentences without changing the meaning (cause, contrast, condition)
Table DI (5 rows × 2–3 columns): percentage increase/decrease of one entity between two years, or one entity as a percentage of another
Table DI with a percentage column (e.g. share of a sub-category): compute derived values (sum, average, difference or ratio of derived quantities)
Caselet DI: a paragraph giving a total and splits in ratios/percentages; questions combine two splits or ask what changes after a transfer
Bar/line-graph DI (values given for 5–6 categories or months): averages, ratios and percentage differences
Missing number series built on differences of squares/cubes, alternate ×n +k, or ×n with increasing n
Wrong number series: one term breaks the ×/+ pattern; find it
Exact simplification with BODMAS, percentages, fractions, squares and square roots; find '?'
Approximation: decimals close to whole numbers in %, ×, ÷, √ and powers; find the nearest value
Find the unknown placed inside the expression (? % of N, √?, ?² or a fraction of ?)
Profit & loss with marked price, discount and cost price (single or successive discounts, 'had he sold for ₹x more')
Percentage word problem: income–expenditure–savings, successive percentage change, or one value as a percentage of another
Ages: present-age ratio with a condition some years before/after; find an age or sum of ages
Ratio & proportion: dividing an amount in a ratio, or changing a ratio by adding/removing a quantity
Time & work / pipes: efficiencies combined, one leaves after some days, or an emptying pipe
Trains crossing poles/platforms/each other, relative speed, or average speed of a round trip
Boats and streams: downstream/upstream speeds and times
Simple vs compound interest: CI–SI difference, amount at CI, or a sum split between two rates
Mixture & alligation: mixing two varieties to a target price/ratio, or adding/replacing liquid
Mensuration: rectangle/circle/cylinder area, perimeter or volume relationships
Average: one member removed/added or replaced, find the new average or the member's value
Linear row of 6–8 persons facing north (occasionally with a vacant seat); direct clues on ends and 'only n persons between'
Circular table (6–8 persons) facing the centre (or some outside); left/right relations and 'second to the left of' questions
Floor-based puzzle (5–8 floors, sometimes two flats per floor) with a second attribute such as colour/city/fruit
Scheduling puzzle: persons/events on days of the week or months (sometimes with dates 1xth/2xth); 'how many between' questions
Box stacking: boxes placed one above another, with colour/item attribute and 'how many boxes between' clues
Comparison puzzle: heights/weights/marks of 5–6 persons with 'more than only' clues; ask rank or a derived value
Syllogism with 2–3 statements and two conclusions, including 'possibility' conclusions; standard five options
Syllogism with 'Only a few' or 'No' statements where a definite 'All' conclusion is the trap
Direct inequality: two or three combined statements, two conclusions to check
Blood relation chain or 'pointing to a photograph' statement; gender ambiguity is the usual trap
Direction & distance: a person walks a path with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and direction from start
Point-based direction: several points given relative to each other; find direction/distance between two of them
Letter coding: word coded by letter shifts / reversal / opposite letters; code a new word
Sentence (Chinese) coding: three or four phrases coded in two-letter codes; find the code of a word by elimination
Order & ranking: positions from both ends of a row/class, total count, or persons between two people
Alphanumeric-symbol arrangement: count elements satisfying a 'preceded by / followed by' condition, or find the nth element from an end
English alphabet positions: nth letter from left/right after rearrangement or reversal; letter-pair series
Letter pairs in a word with as many letters between them as in the English alphabet
Odd one out among numbers, words or letter groups

resources.notes: SBI does not publish Junior Associate question papers or answer keys. The official advertisement (with exam pattern) and pre-examination training material for eligible candidates are on sbi.bank.in/web/careers. Previous papers circulating online are memory-based compilations by coaching portals.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Millets were once a staple across much of India, but after the Green Revolution they were steadily replaced by rice and wheat, which received assured procurement and gave higher yields. Millets, however, need far less water, tolerate heat and grow well on poor soils. As groundwater levels fall and summers grow hotter, these qualities have attracted fresh attention. Several states now include millets in school meals and public distribution, hoping to create steady demand. Farmers say that demand alone is not enough: they also need better seeds, processing units close to villages and fair prices. Without these, they argue, millets will remain a niche product admired in seminars but rarely seen on dinner plates.

Which of the following is NOT stated about millets in the passage?
options: They are resistant to all pests
They grow well on poor soils
questions.explanation: Water, heat tolerance, poor soils and fresh attention are mentioned; pest resistance is not.

relevance.note: NOT-stated with invented 'resistant to all pests' overstatement; good E02

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
My brother, who lives in Pune, (A)/ is elder than (B)/ me by three years (C)/ and works in a bank. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Elder' is not followed by 'than'; the correct form is 'older than'. Error in part B.

relevance.note: 'elder than' vs 'older than'; classic clerk trap

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks.
The manager ______ the proposal because it was not ______ with the bank's policy.
questions.explanation: A proposal not consistent with policy is rejected. 'Not accordance with' is ungrammatical, and accepting/welcoming contradicts 'because it was not…'.

relevance.note: Double filler with 'accordance' half-fit trap; good

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
A. He noticed that many elderly neighbours struggled to use mobile banking.
B. Arjun, a college student, spent his summer holidays at home.
C. So he started free weekend classes in the community hall.
D. By the end of the summer, over forty seniors could pay bills on their own.
E. Some of them even depended on strangers to complete simple payments.
questions.explanation: B (introduces Arjun) → A (what he noticed) → E (how bad it was) → C (his response) → D (result): BAECD.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph and choose the LAST sentence.
A. Rinse the seeds and soak them overnight.
B. Next morning, drain the water and tie the seeds in a wet cloth.
C. Sprouts are a cheap and healthy addition to any meal.
D. Within a day or two, small shoots will appear.
E. Making them at home is simple.
questions.explanation: Order: C – E – A – B – D. The last sentence is D.

relevance.note: Recipe-like jumble LAST sentence; clear markers

Each of the players HAVE BEEN GIVEN a new kit.
questions.explanation: 'Each of the players' is singular and the sense is passive: 'has been given'.

Six persons G, H, I, J, K and L sit in a row of seven seats facing north; one seat is vacant. The vacant seat is third from the left end. H sits second to the right of the vacant seat. Only one seat lies between H and I. K sits next to I. L sits immediately to the right of the vacant seat. G does not sit at either end.

Who sits at the extreme left end?
questions.explanation: Seats 1–7 (left to right): J, G, vacant, L, H, K, I. Vacant = 3, L = 4, H = 5, I = 7 (seat 3 is vacant), K = 6; G is not at an end so G = 2 and J = 1.

relevance.note: 7-seat row with vacant seat, unique J G _ L H K I

questions.question:
Six persons G, H, I, J, K and L sit in a row of seven seats facing north; one seat is vacant. The vacant seat is third from the left end. H sits second to the right of the vacant seat. Only one seat lies between H and I. K sits next to I. L sits immediately to the right of the vacant seat. G does not sit at either end.

How many persons sit between G and K?
questions.explanation: Seats: J, G, vacant, L, H, K, I. Between G (2) and K (6) are seat 3 (vacant), L and H — two persons.

relevance.note: Persons between G and K counting vacancy trap (2)

questions.question:
Six persons G, H, I, J, K and L sit in a row of seven seats facing north; one seat is vacant. The vacant seat is third from the left end. H sits second to the right of the vacant seat. Only one seat lies between H and I. K sits next to I. L sits immediately to the right of the vacant seat. G does not sit at either end.

Who sits immediately to the left of H?
questions.explanation: Seats: J, G, vacant, L, H, K, I. Facing north, left means the lower-numbered seat; L (seat 4) is immediately left of H (seat 5).

questions.question:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E live on five different floors of a building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 5 the top), and each likes a different colour — Red, Blue, Green, White and Pink. B lives on the top floor. Only one person lives between B and A. D likes Blue and lives immediately below B. C lives on a floor below E. E likes Red. The one who likes Green lives on an odd-numbered floor above A. A does not like White.

Who likes Pink?
questions.explanation: Floors 1→5: C-White, E-Red, A-Pink, D-Blue, B-Green. A likes Pink.

questions.question:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E live on five different floors of a building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 5 the top), and each likes a different colour — Red, Blue, Green, White and Pink. B lives on the top floor. Only one person lives between B and A. D likes Blue and lives immediately below B. C lives on a floor below E. E likes Red. The one who likes Green lives on an odd-numbered floor above A. A does not like White.

Which colour is liked by the person who lives on floor 1?
questions.explanation: B is on 5, D (Blue) on 4, A on 3; C below E gives C on 1 and E on 2. Green is on an odd floor above A → floor 5 (B). A is not White, so A is Pink and C is White.

questions.question:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E live on five different floors of a building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 5 the top), and each likes a different colour — Red, Blue, Green, White and Pink. B lives on the top floor. Only one person lives between B and A. D likes Blue and lives immediately below B. C lives on a floor below E. E likes Red. The one who likes Green lives on an odd-numbered floor above A. A does not like White.

How many persons live between C and D?
questions.explanation: Floors 1→5: C, E, A, D, B. Between C (1) and D (4) are E and A — two persons.

questions.question:
Statements: No laptop is a phone. Some phones are tablets.
Conclusions: I. Some tablets are not laptops. II. Some laptops are tablets.
questions.explanation: The tablets that are phones cannot be laptops, so I follows. II is only a possibility.

relevance.note: No/Some 'Some tablets are not laptops'; standard

questions.question:
Statement: P < Q = R ≤ S < T
Conclusions: I. T > Q  II. P < S
questions.explanation: T > S ≥ R = Q gives T > Q; P < Q = R ≤ S gives P < S. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: K ≥ L > M; N ≥ L; O < M
Conclusions: I. N > O  II. K > N
questions.explanation: N ≥ L > M > O gives N > O. K and N are both ≥ L, so no relation between them. Only I follows.

relevance.note: Branch inequality, K vs N undetermined

questions.question: In a code language, 'bank loan approved' is written as 'ra si te', 'loan is pending' as 'te po mu' and 'approved is final' as 'mu si ka'. What is the code for 'pending'?
questions.explanation: loan = te (1 & 2), approved = si (1 & 3), is = mu (2 & 3). In 'loan is pending', the remaining code po = pending.

questions.question: Introducing a man, Neha said, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is Neha related to the man?
questions.explanation: The only daughter of Neha's mother is Neha herself, so Neha is the man's mother.

relevance.note: Only daughter of my mother = herself; classic trap

questions.question: In a queue, Amit is 12th from the front and Sunil is 18th from the back. Exactly four persons stand between them. What is the maximum possible number of persons in the queue?
questions.explanation: Maximum when Amit is ahead of Sunil with 4 persons between: 12 + 4 + 18 = 34.

relevance.note: Max queue size with fixed gap; good trap

questions.question:
Arrangement: R 4 T # 8 L @ 2 M 6 % N 9 & P 3 K
How many numbers are immediately followed by a symbol?
questions.explanation: Only 6 (followed by %) and 9 (followed by &) qualify — two.

questions.question: How many pairs of letters in the word 'CAPITAL' have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (in either direction)?
questions.explanation: P–L (3 letters between in both: I, T, A and M, N, O) and I–L (2 between: T, A and J, K). Two pairs.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

In villages where newspapers arrive late and television offers little local news, community radio has quietly become a lifeline. These small stations, run by local groups and broadcasting within a radius of a few kilometres, speak in the dialect of their listeners and talk about matters that big channels ignore — the price of onions at the nearest market, the date of the next vaccination camp, or a warning about an approaching storm.

Because the presenters are often farmers, teachers or homemakers from the same area, listeners trust them. During floods, some stations have stayed on air through the night, helping families locate relatives and guiding them to relief camps. Others run programmes in which elderly residents record folk songs and stories that might otherwise be lost.

Running a station, however, is not easy. Most depend on small grants and local advertisements, and many struggle to pay for equipment repairs or to keep trained volunteers. Supporters argue that a little steady funding would allow these stations to grow into reliable sources of information for the communities they serve.

Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Community radio gives villages trusted local information but needs steady funding to survive
Television has completely replaced radio in Indian villages
Community radio stations earn large profits from advertisements
Big news channels cover village markets in great detail
Folk songs are the most popular programmes on all radio stations
questions.explanation: The passage describes how community radio serves villages and is trusted, and then explains that it struggles for money and needs steady funding.

questions.question:

questions.question:
Seven persons P, Q, R, S, T, U and V sit around a circular table, all facing the centre.
Q sits second to the right of P. R sits immediately to the left of Q. S sits third to the left of R. T is not an immediate neighbour of S. U sits immediately to the right of S.

Who sits third to the right of T?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P: P, U, S, V, T, Q, R (for persons facing the centre, left is clockwise). Counting anticlockwise from T: V, S, U — U is third to the right of T.

Q sits second to the right of P. R sits immediately to the left of Q. S sits third to the left of R. T is not an immediate neighbour of S. U sits immediately to the right of S.

Who sits between S and T?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P: P, U, S, V, T, Q, R (for persons facing the centre, left is clockwise). V sits between S and T.

questions.question:
Seven persons P, Q, R, S, T, U and V sit around a circular table, all facing the centre.
Q sits second to the right of P. R sits immediately to the left of Q. S sits third to the left of R. T is not an immediate neighbour of S. U sits immediately to the right of S.

What is the position of Q with respect to V?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P: P, U, S, V, T, Q, R (for persons facing the centre, left is clockwise). From V, moving clockwise (to the left): T, Q — Q is second to the left of V.

questions.question:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F were born in six different months — January, February, March, April, May and June — of the same year.
C was born in a month that has 30 days. Only two persons were born between C and A. F was born immediately after A. E was born in a month that has 31 days. B was born after E. D was born before A.

Who was born in May?
questions.explanation: January – E, February – D, March – A, April – F, May – B, June – C. (C in April would force A into January, leaving no month before A for D.) B was born in May.

questions.question:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F were born in six different months — January, February, March, April, May and June — of the same year.
C was born in a month that has 30 days. Only two persons were born between C and A. F was born immediately after A. E was born in a month that has 31 days. B was born after E. D was born before A.

How many persons were born between E and F?
questions.explanation: January – E, February – D, March – A, April – F, May – B, June – C. (C in April would force A into January, leaving no month before A for D.) D and A were born between E (January) and F (April).

questions.question:
Statements: All chairs are tables. No table is a bed.
Conclusions: I. No chair is a bed. II. Some beds are chairs.
questions.explanation: All chairs are tables and no table is a bed, so no chair is a bed — I follows and II is false.

questions.question:
Statements: Some keys are locks. Some locks are doors.
Conclusions: I. Some keys are doors. II. No key is a door.
questions.explanation: Neither conclusion is definite on its own, but they form a complementary pair ('some' / 'no') about the same terms, so one of them must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.question:
Statement: A > B ≥ C = D < E
Conclusions: I. B ≥ D  II. E > C
questions.explanation: B ≥ C = D gives B ≥ D. E > D = C gives E > C. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: K ≤ L < M; N > M ≥ O
Conclusions: I. N > K  II. O > L
questions.explanation: N > M > L ≥ K gives N > K. O ≤ M and L < M give no relation between O and L. Only I follows.

questions.question: In a code language, 'red green blue' is written as 'ka pa ta', 'green yellow pink' is written as 'pa ra na' and 'blue pink black' is written as 'ta na sa'. What is the code for 'yellow'?
questions.explanation: green = pa (sentences 1 and 2), blue = ta (1 and 3), pink = na (2 and 3). The remaining code in sentence 2, 'ra', means 'yellow'.

questions.question:
Study the arrangement:
5 A # 7 K @ 3 L M 9 % B 2 & D 6 $ F 8
How many numbers are immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a symbol?
questions.explanation: Qualifying numbers: 9 (M 9 %), 2 (B 2 &) and 6 (D 6 $). 7 is preceded by # and 3 by @. Total = 3.

questions.question: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'MONEY' which have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (in either direction)?
questions.explanation: Only O–N qualifies (adjacent in the word and in the alphabet). No other pair matches.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Video consultations have made city hospitals unnecessary for villagers.
Telemedicine saves rural patients time and money, but it works best when trained local health workers support it.
Weak internet is the only obstacle to telemedicine in villages.
Elderly patients in villages refuse to consult doctors by video.
Kamla Devi's grandson was cured without consulting any doctor.
questions.explanation: The passage weighs the gains of telemedicine against its limits and concludes it works best as a tool in the hands of local health workers. The other options overstate one detail or contradict the passage (the grandson did consult a doctor by video).

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: The doctor asked the nurse to take the child to the district town.
Video consultations in villages are always free of cost.
All illnesses can be judged accurately through a video consultation.
A trip to a city hospital may mean losing a day's wages.
Elderly patients prefer video consultations to a visit to town.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a trip to a city hospital often means losing a day's wages. The consultation costs 'little or nothing' (not always free), some illnesses need a physical examination, and elderly patients prefer to wait for a visit to town.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a limitation of telemedicine?
options: Medicines prescribed by video are not available in villages.
A doctor on a screen cannot physically examine the patient.
Weak internet in hilly areas can cut consultations short.
Some elderly patients are uncomfortable with a doctor they cannot meet.
Some illnesses need laboratory tests before they can be judged.
questions.explanation: The passage actually says the medicines were available at the village centre itself; the other four limitations are stated in paragraph 3.

questions.question:
Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
I. Where health assistants are poorly trained, fewer patients are likely to keep using telemedicine.
II. Most patients in remote areas have stopped using telemedicine because of weak internet.
III. Video consultations can reduce the number of trips villagers make to city hospitals.
questions.explanation: I: 'where they are not [well trained], people soon lose faith'. III: the family avoided the journey to town by using the village centre. II overstates — weak internet 'can cut a consultation short', but nothing says most patients have stopped.

questions.question: Which of the following is most similar in meaning to the word 'judged' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Some illnesses cannot be judged without tests' means they cannot be assessed. 'Sentenced' (court) and 'criticised' are dictionary meanings that do not fit; 'guessed' is a near miss but means the opposite of a careful judgement.

questions.question: Which of the following is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'accurately' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: To take readings 'accurately' is to take them correctly and exactly; the opposite is 'imprecisely'. 'Carefully' is close in meaning, not opposite.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (1)?
questions.explanation: With QR payments, the problem of loose change has largely 'disappeared'. The other verbs need an object and do not make sense with 'problem … has largely ___'.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (2)?
questions.explanation: The payment record helps sellers 'prove' that they run a steady business. 'Disprove' gives the opposite sense; 'approve', 'improve' and 'reprove' (scold) are look-alikes.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (3)?
questions.explanation: 'Access to formal credit' is the correct collocation. 'Excess' and 'assess' are sound-alike traps; 'success' and 'process' do not take 'to credit'.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (4)?
questions.explanation: 'Check their accounts' takes a direct object. 'Look' and 'glance' need 'at', and 'notice/see their accounts to see' is not idiomatic.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (5)?
questions.explanation: Sound-boxes help to 'curb' (restrain) cheating. 'Curve', 'carve', 'crave' and 'curl' are look-alike words with unrelated meanings.

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (6)?
questions.explanation: Awareness will be as 'important' as the technology itself. The other words look similar but do not make sense in the comparison.

questions.question: Which of the following will be the FIRST sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: Correct order: B E A F C D. B introduces Ravi and the tin box; every other sentence depends on it.

questions.question: Which of the following will be the THIRD sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: B (savings in a tin box) → E (flood soaks the shelves) → A (notes found damp when the box is opened) → F (bank exchanges some notes) → C ('the experience' leads him to open an account) → D (now earns interest). Third is A.

questions.question: Which of the following will be the FIFTH sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: Order B E A F C D: 'The experience' in C refers to the loss described in F, and D ('Now his money earns interest') must follow the opening of the account in C. Fifth is C.

questions.question: Which of the following will be the LAST (SIXTH) sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: Order B E A F C D. D describes the present outcome and closes the paragraph.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
Neither of the two cashiers (A)/ were present at the counter (B)/ when the customer arrived (C)/ to deposit the cash. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb: 'Neither of the two cashiers was present'. The error is in part B.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
The manager asked me that why (A)/ I had not submitted (B)/ the account opening form (C)/ before the due date. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: In indirect speech a wh-question is not introduced by 'that': 'The manager asked me why I had not submitted…'. The error is in part A.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
The bank has decided (A)/ to waive the processing charges (B)/ on loans for senior citizens (C)/ who are above the age of seventy. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct: 'decided to waive', 'charges on loans' and 'above the age of seventy' are all standard usage.

questions.question:
Choose the pair of words that best fills both blanks.
The bank ______ its branch timings so that working people could ______ their transactions in the evening.
questions.explanation: Longer timings let working people complete transactions in the evening. In each other pair one word breaks the logic: reduced/shortened/closed contradict 'in the evening', and 'avoid' contradicts the purpose.

questions.question:
Choose the pair of words that best fills both blanks.
Heavy rain ______ the supply of vegetables to the city, and prices ______ sharply within a week.
questions.explanation: Disrupted supply pushes prices up. 'Improved'/'increased' supply would not follow heavy rain, and 'fell'/'declined' contradict a supply disruption.

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct. If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
If the customer HAD ASKED FOR a receipt, he would have been able to claim the refund.
questions.explanation: A third-conditional sentence uses 'If + had + past participle … would have + past participle'. 'Had asked for' is already correct.

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct. If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Hardly had he reached the platform THAN THE TRAIN LEFT.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly … when' is the correct pair (not 'than', which goes with 'no sooner'). The simple past 'left' is right after 'had reached'.

questions.question: Which box is kept immediately above the Green box?
questions.explanation: Stack from top: 8 T–Brown, 7 P–Grey, 6 W–Red, 5 R–Blue, 4 V–Green, 3 Q–White, 2 U–Yellow, 1 S–Black. Q must be at 3 (with V at 4, P at 7, T at 8; S at 1, U at 2; R–W at 5–6). Green is V (4); R at 5 is immediately above.

questions.question: How many boxes are kept between U and the Grey box?
questions.explanation: Grey must be above Blue (5) but Red is at 6 and Brown must be immediately above Grey, so Grey is at 7 (P) and Brown at 8. U is at 2; positions 3, 4, 5 and 6 lie between — four boxes.

questions.question: What is the colour of box Q?
questions.explanation: White must be two places from Blue (5), i.e. at 3 or 7; 7 is Grey, so White is at 3, which is Q. (Green at 4 is immediately above it.)

questions.question: Which of the following box – colour pairs is correct?
questions.explanation: Positions 1 and 2 (S and U) take Yellow and Black, with Yellow above Black, so S (1) is Black and U (2) is Yellow. Only 'S – Black' is correct.

questions.question: If the boxes are rearranged in alphabetical order from bottom to top (P at position 1, W at position 8), how many boxes will remain at their original positions?
questions.explanation: Original positions: P7, Q3, R5, S1, T8, U2, V4, W6. Alphabetical order would put P1, Q2, R3, S4, T5, U6, V7, W8 — no box keeps its position.

passages.title: Reading comprehension: telemedicine in villages
passages.text:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

When Kamla Devi's grandson developed a high fever last winter, the nearest specialist was in a district town three hours away by bus. Instead of making the journey, the family walked to the health centre in their village, where a nurse connected them by video to a doctor in the city. The doctor examined the child's symptoms on screen, asked the nurse to check his pulse and temperature, and prescribed medicines that were available at the centre itself.

Stories like this have become more common as health centres in rural areas are linked to doctors through the internet. For patients, the biggest gain is the saving of time and money. A trip to a city hospital often means losing a day's wages, paying for travel and sometimes staying overnight. A video consultation in the village costs little or nothing.

However, telemedicine is not a cure for every problem. A doctor on a screen cannot touch a patient, and some illnesses cannot be judged without a physical examination or laboratory tests. Weak internet connections in hilly and remote areas can cut a consultation short. Many elderly patients are also uncomfortable speaking to a doctor they cannot meet in person, and prefer to wait for a visit to town.

Health workers say that the success of the system depends largely on the nurse or health assistant who sits with the patient. A trained assistant can describe symptoms clearly, take readings accurately and explain the doctor's advice in the local language. Where such assistants are well trained, patients return; where they are not, people soon lose faith in the screen. Telemedicine, in other words, works best not as a replacement for local health workers but as a tool in their hands.

passages.title: Cloze passage: digital payments at small shops
passages.text:
Read the passage carefully. Each numbered blank has a question below it.

A few years ago, a vegetable seller in a small town would have laughed at the idea of accepting payment through a mobile phone. Today, a printed QR code hangs from almost every cart, and the old problem of loose change has largely (1) ______. For the sellers, the benefits go beyond convenience. Every digital payment leaves a record, and over time this record helps them (2) ______ that they run a steady business. Some banks now use such records to offer small loans to traders who earlier had no (3) ______ to formal credit.

The change, however, has also brought new risks. Fraudsters sometimes show fake payment messages, and busy sellers do not always (4) ______ their accounts to see whether the money has actually arrived. Sound-box devices that announce each payment aloud have helped to (5) ______ such cheating. As digital payments spread further, simple awareness about safe practices will be as (6) ______ as the technology itself.

passages.title: Para jumble: sentences A–F
passages.text:
The following six sentences A, B, C, D, E and F are given in a jumbled order. Rearrange them to form a meaningful paragraph and answer the questions that follow.

A. By the time he opened the box, most of the notes inside had become damp and torn.
B. Ravi had always kept his savings in a tin box hidden in the kitchen.
C. The experience convinced him to open a savings account the very next week.
D. Now his money earns interest, and he no longer worries about floods or thieves.
E. One monsoon night, water entered the house and soaked everything on the lower shelves.
F. The bank exchanged the damaged notes that could still be identified, but he lost a part of his money.

passages.title: Puzzle: eight boxes in a stack
passages.text:
Study the following information carefully and answer the questions given below.

Eight boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are kept one above another in a single stack. The bottommost position is numbered 1 and the topmost position is numbered 8. Each box is of a different colour among Brown, Grey, Red, Blue, Green, White, Yellow and Black.

Only two boxes are kept between P and V. V is kept immediately above Q, and Q is kept at an odd-numbered position. Only one box is kept between Q and S. T is kept immediately above P. R is kept immediately below W. U is kept somewhere below Q. Box W is Red. The Red box is kept immediately above the Blue box. Only one box is kept between the Blue box and the White box. The Green box is kept immediately above the White box. The Grey box is kept somewhere above the Blue box, and the Brown box is kept immediately above the Grey box. The Yellow box is kept somewhere above the Black box.
